3 I am sorry... see you. She feared for the health of her dearest Vincenza. She expressed her misgivings to Sr. A. Francesca. Cf. L 54,2.

4 She sometimes feels unwell and is sorry when she is taken ill in front of people she has to deal with.

5 The Superior of the Mother House is Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini.

She invites her to come to her by carriage. She is worried about Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino's health.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. For charity's sake don't write to the Superior, because it would do harm; you will hear by word of mouth.2 My God, so many things! I hope you will come soon; take care of yourself.

  2. I don't like the look of Sr. A. Vincenza at all; I fear she will go the way of poor Delaide. This thought is killing me, it gives me no rest.3 More in person.

  3. If you come, try to come by carriage; have it come to your door, and so here to S. Donato.4

Goodbye, your affect. M. R.

1 This appears to be the date, the Mother having arrived in Genoa the day before. Cf. L53 and 51,3.

2 She is probably referring to the Superior of the Genoa House, Sr. A. Santina Solenghi.

3 ...go the way... no rest. She has a sad foreboding that the same will happen to her as to poor Sr. A. Adelaide, who did not survive her illness. She was not wrong. Sr. A. Vincenza had barely a month to live. She died on 3 April 1875.

4 With motherly understanding and tact, knowing she was in poor health, she advises her not to walk: from the Sampierdarena hospital to Genoa, Via S. Donato, where she was staying, always by carriage.

She is worried about Alessandro, who she hears is involved with a woman of ill repute and has signed two bills of exchange. She suggests she advise him on the matter. She has been ill with a «frightful bronchitis» and is now up.

A.M.F. My Onorata,

  1. I am writing to you on my knees, with anguish in my soul over certain matters concerning Alessandro which are very painful to me, and which you alone must know, so that you can try to remedy what may happen.

  2. Listen, Acc. insists that while I was in Piacenza Alessandro ran off with that horrid woman and went with her to Genoa, because this wretched creature is always tormenting him and is now plying her ugly... my God!1

  3. You must also know that two bills of exchange have come to light, made out with Alessandro and others.2 Who enjoyed the money they will know, but since Alessandro is under age they cannot touch him at all; only I would not want him to make any written promises. He is out of all danger because, as I tell you, he is not of age; so he must turn a deaf ear to everything and not reply to any of the threats they may make.3 For charity's sake, try to persuade him that they are all rogues; I use this word because if you had heard how they got him to make them, or rather how they made them, it is dreadful.

  4. So, dear Onorata, try to find out everything they have written to him; I fear Alessandro may let himself [be drawn] into something;4 I should also like you to point out to him that he must not squander money, because he is a real bottomless pit of extravagance and will not consider his position at all;5 for charity's sake.

  5. I hope you have received the vegetables; today I am sending you a basket of fish and two of pasta.

  6. Give me news of Sr. A. Vincenza; I find it hard to write and I am alone, so to speak; I had a frightful bronchitis that brought me very low. I am up, but I cough all the time and am extremely weak.

  7. The lawsuit has been heard; now I am awaiting the decision.6 Read this as best you can.

  8. I assure you these affairs of Alessandro's grieve me to the heart. Yesterday one of these bills; I suffered greatly; I hope he does not do anything as foolish as letting the chain and watch go.7 I beg you, he must stand firm and not reply. Yesterday I was advised: if they dare to come, send them away saying he has nothing;8 in this way it will all end. Onorata, I beg you.

Goodbye, yours for ever

Affect. Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 Listen, Acc. insists... God! She has learned from Fr Antonio Accinelli that Alessandro has had a relationship with a woman of ill repute who works as a prostitute. Onorata replies on the following 17 March, defending the young man's innocence with good and credible reasons.

2 Alessandro had signed two bills of exchange. Onorata, after questioning him, explains in the same letter: «Alessandro left no other muddles there than the bill for 300 lire, of which he says he enjoyed nothing. Just listen to the roguery! He left 50 lire with the moneylender for three months' interest, gave 10 lire to the broker, 25 lire to the man who had suggested the bright idea of the bill, and with the rest he was taken to a café where, egged on by bad company, at the game of caratella, a game he did not know at all, he was stripped that same evening of his last penny and went home with empty pockets and remorse at having done wrong...».

3 Alessandro is under age... make. He was 20 and therefore could not be prosecuted. He was not to pay or worry about any threats the creditors might make.

4 ...try to find out... something. Onorata replies that she will collect all the correspondence herself and that she and her family will know how to defend the young man.

5 I should like... position. Alessandro is a spendthrift and will not take his own financial situation into account at all.

6 The lawsuit with Fr Angelo Ricchino. Cf. L 24, n. 6; 67; 68.

7 I hope he does not do anything as foolish as selling or pawning the watch and chain.

8 If the creditors dare to appear, she is to send them away, explaining the young man's position.

She begs him not to pay the bill of exchange. She has taken advice from competent people. She herself will see to paying off the debt. He is to stand firm and keep to what she has written. If he really disagrees, he is to let her know.

A.M.F. My Alessandro,

  1. I beg you for the love of God not to get it into your head to pay the bill on the spot;1 I have no money; it would mean taking that very small capital Accinelli holds, which is reduced to the minimum; so I took advice, and was advised not to pay and indeed to stand firm, because this is money that was handled by others, not by you, and since you are not of age they cannot do you the slightest harm.2

  2. Moreover, we have this gentleman's girl boarding with us, which is paid for little by little, because I shall keep her without charging anything; so the Fr. 300 will soon be paid. See, at 20 F. a month, in a year and 4 months it is paid off. Do you think that is all right?3

  3. I am truly in despair, because I do not know where to lay my head; troubles come crowding upon me and I feel I can bear no more. You obey; turn a deaf ear to all the letters and threats, which are worthless, because the law protects you. Since you are not of age, they can do nothing, nothing to you.4 Rest easy; they are all bogeymen.

  4. I have made thorough enquiries; they try everything, they go to your uncles, they come to me, to Accinelli, and knowing they have no power at all, they try every avenue. Alessandro, stand firm, for pity's sake, because you see that this Gentleman will be paid little by little; I do not know where to find the money.

  5. Write to me at once, or rather, tell me whether you are happy with what I have done.5 I have written to Onorata, sending the letter registered.6 I find myself with heavy commitments and do not know how to get out of them. I receive not a penny from anywhere; tell me if you are happy; I thought I was doing right, but if you are not happy, write and tell me and I shall try to do as you wish.7

  6. Goodbye; I write to you in the depths of sorrow, because at this moment other afflictions come to pierce me, and I still cannot manage to sit at the desk; I am writing to you on my knees.8

your most affect. M. R. Gattorno

1 To pay on the spot, that is, at once. Cf. L 55, n. 2.

2 // minimo scorno: harm.

3 She has thus found a way of paying off the bill, having no means of paying at once in cash.

4 She repeats what she has already said, to convince him.

5 Tell me whether you are happy. She knew her Alessandro well and how much honesty and his good name mattered to him.

6 It is the previous letter (L 55), sent registered.

7 Write and tell me. She wants to stop Alessandro from solving the problem on his own.

8 She used the same expression with Onorata. She had just recovered from a serious bronchitis. Cf. L 55,6.

She categorically forbids her to offer herself to God as a victim for Vincenza's health or her own. She is to take care of herself and get well.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. First of all I forbid you to offer yourself to God, whether for Sr. A. Vincenza, or for me,2 or for anyone else; indeed I declare, with all the authority God has given me over the Daughters of Saint Anne and over you in particular, that I do not want your offerings to be heard; on the contrary, under Holy Obedience, ask God's pardon and tell Him that you want to get well and live a hundred years because of the obedience you owe me; so I will it, so be it.3

  2. Stop uttering heresies once and for all;4 be cheerful and you will live. Sr. A. Vincenza is getting better, and I hope the good Lord will restore her to full health; I am better, indeed I am well, and I hope to come and see you. Try to get well and take the decoction; it cured me, I have no more cough, I am well.5 Ah! If Sr. A. Vincenza had had faith and accepted it, she would have been cured.

Your affect. M. R...

1 This letter is dated Genoa, 21.3.73. Since at that time the Mother was in Rome and not Genoa, and bearing in mind the context and facts, it can be assigned to 1875.

2 She forbids her to offer her life to God in place of that of Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino, who was seriously ill (cf. L 54,2), or her own, as she too was ill at that time, cf. L 55,6.

3 The tone is firm and solemn. The prohibition is formal: «under Holy Obedience» she must ask God's pardon and ask Him for healing.

4 Heresies: God, a loving Father, wills the life and not the death of His children.

5 // decotto. It was prepared for her by Signora Maddalena Bacigalupo. The Mother had several times experienced its healing properties.

She asks for news of Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino's treatment and health.

My daughter,

  1. I have received your letter. For charity's sake, I hear you are mixing pills and decoction; be very careful what you are doing.2

  2. I should like to know whether the issues look good, whether they are discharging; and also what the sputum is like.3

  3. For charity's sake, don't tire yourself too much on those stairs; call someone, have things carried. Tell Anna, regarding what she put in her letter about paying for her board, I do not want her to talk about it, otherwise she will displease me.4 How is Sr. A. Vincenza? Is she taking the oil?5

Goodbye, yours for ever affect. M. R.

God bless you.

1 This letter is dated 25.2.75 but is certainly from March. The Mother, being in Genoa and unable to go to Piacenza for health reasons, sent Sr. A. Santina to nurse Vincenza.

2 In her letter of 25 March Santina informs her of the patient's condition and the remedies used. The decoction: cf. L 57, n. 5.

3 I should like to know whether the issues are working well. Issues or cauteries: openings made in the flesh with a caustic to let out the humours. She also wants to know what the sputum is like. Sr. A. Vincenza had tuberculosis.

4 Anna Grasso (cf. L 6, n. 6) wanted to stay as a guest at the Mother House; she had written that she wished to pay for her board.

5 Is she taking the olive oil blessed by Mother Rosa following an inspiration she received from the Eternal Father while praying. It was called the oil of the Eternal Father.

She gives precise orders on how the Sisters are to behave towards Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino and her mother.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Here are my orders. I command and will that none of the religious go into Sr. A. Vincenza's room. I want no one to go in except Sr. A. Santina and Sr. A. Costanza, and no one else. I absolutely do not want the nuns to linger upstairs, none in the little study, not one, for charity's sake;2 and woe to any religious who stops to talk to Signora Rapallino!3

  2. I am tired of gossip; I don't want to hear any more; from the portress to the cook, I insist that they do not talk to outsiders. So these two alone are to nurse Sr. A. Vincenza and no one else. Oh! how much reaches me through the wicked tongues of nuns!4

  3. Send for the bricklayer and have a stove put in Sr. A. Vincenza's room at once, and tell Signora Rapallino that I have no better room for her daughter, because my little study is too small for her, as she suffers from breathlessness.5 So the master builder is to buy one at once and install it; spare no expense. I cannot understand how my little study is also used for recreation and a bit of everything; enough.6 I am not able to come, being too weak.7

I am yours, in haste, your

Affect. M.R.

1 The date is missing and is inferred from the context.

2 The orders are given for reasons of hygiene and prudence, the disease being infectious. Only Sr. A. Santina and Sr. A. Costanza Cenni, the two nurses, could enter the sick woman's room.

3 Signora Bianca Rapallino, Sr. A. Vincenza's mother, had hurried to be with her daughter.

4 Sr. A. Vincenza was known and loved in Piacenza. Everyone asked for news and received inaccurate reports from people not well informed about the situation. Rumours reached Genoa — how much reaches me through the wicked tongues of nuns!

5 The Mother's study had a wood stove, but it was too small to take the sick woman's bed, as Signora Rapallino had proposed.

6 The Superior and the Sisters gathered in the Mother's study every evening for recreation. Cf. L to M. Rosa from Sr. A. Santina Solenghi of 26.3.75.

7 Cf. L 55,6.

She tells her that the next day she will receive a letter with a note for Sr. A. Vincenza.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. I am letting you know that tomorrow you should receive a letter addressed to you, and inside there is one for Sr. A. Vincenza,2 in which I told her to get well and do the obedience, for I intend her breathlessness to stop at once, as I hope she will be better.

Goodbye, be careful, for charity's sake

your affect. M. R.

1 The date is clearly inferred from the following letter, published here as no. 61.

2 Cf. L61/7.

She suggests how to behave in nursing Sr. A. Vincenza and what to answer those who criticise what she is doing. She is to give the enclosed note to the patient.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

  1. I have just received a letter from you and hear what you tell me about Sr. A. Vincenza.1 Yes, courage; I urge you to give her the oil of the Eternal Father, and when she coughs, rub her throat with it if she cannot swallow it, but as soon as she can, a teaspoonful, at once; faith.2

  2. For charity's sake, don't tell anyone about it, as you did with the decoction;3 luckily I hear you have finished it, otherwise I would be anxious. Mixing the decoction with the doctor's medicines, my God! for charity's sake! Enough. I hear she is better; give her these two [lines].4

  3. Laugh at them all, and when she sends for you, laugh and answer her: «What do you want? I am under obedience and must do this; when I receive another order, then I shall carry it out. For now I shall not depart from obedience. Rest assured that I do nothing on my own initiative; and I am sure you will believe me; but if you do not believe me, write to the one down there and you will see whether I am telling the truth».5

  4. Listen, before you leave, ask for four Crucifixes for those here who don't have one; and if you need anything else you can do the same; get them to give you them.

  5. «It is time to get up — you will tell Sr. A. Vincenza — and to do the Obedience».

  6. Greet everyone for me. I am not writing because I am weak; I

urge you to keep the oil hidden.6 Goodbye! Courage, don't trouble yourself, for charity's sake don't wear yourself out.

Your affect. M. R.

7. These two lines for Sr. A. Vincenza: once she has read them, tell her to give them back to you, sealed in another envelope, because you know very well that when making the bed or moving about they might fall out, and woe to anyone who saw them! I rely on you, for charity's sake!

1 In her L of 26 March she gave her detailed news of the course of the illness, expressing optimism.

2 More than to medicines, the Mother appealed to faith in God the Father. Cf. L 58, n. 5.

3 As for the decoction against catarrh, they had decided to give it only in the morning; during the day they gave her the pills prescribed by the doctor.

4 give her these two lines. Cf. L 60,1 and paragraph 7 below.

5 Laugh at them all... the truth. In the house they were finding fault with Sr. A. Santina's nursing of Sr. A. Vincenza. The Mother's advice: laugh, that is, don't worry, don't take what they say seriously, and when the Superior sends for you, answer her cheerfully and calmly that you are following my advice and obeying me. Let them write to me (the one down there, in Genoa).

6 The oil of the Eternal Father mentioned above, paragraph 1.

She has heard that Sr. A. Vincenza is better and hopes for steady recovery. She is to try to return to Genoa to free her from her commitments to the community.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Yesterday, from the telegrams Signora Rapallino sent her husband, I see that the patient is better; so listen, see whether you can come down, because I really need you; leave Sr. A. Costanza there and you come, because otherwise I am too tied,1 and besides there are so many things to do; so see about coming, especially as this week the oaths are to be taken.2

  2. Do everything you can to come as soon as possible; Signora Rapallino, it [seems] to me, will be enough with one nurse, and so you can manage it. I hope Sr. A. Vincenza will not relapse and will go on improving.

  3. I am anxious because I have not received the Father's letter which you say told me everything about Sr. A. Vincenza; tell him it has been lost;3 for charity's sake, be careful how you post them.

Goodbye, greet Sr. A. Vincenza for me and tell her she must obey absolutely.

your affect. M. R.

1 The Mother, besides dealing with the Institute's problems, was standing in for the Superior, Santina. Cf. L 63,5.

2 Fr Angelo Ricchino had asked, to settle the case, for a further statement from the Mother and Fr Tornatore under oath. Cf. L 67 and 68.

3 Unfortunately some letters had gone astray.

Advice on her duties as Superior of the House and instructions for two Sisters' journey to Pennabilli.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just received your letter in which you say you wrote me another on the 27th; I have not received it and I am anxious,1 because I know nothing of whether you received the Sisters who left for Pennabilli. I cannot understand how letters get lost.2

  2. You tell me that this Lady goes into the kitchen; I am amazed that you have given her such free rein; what, she goes into the kitchen? Alas! for pity's sake I would not want her to meddle in these matters, because when she wants something she must ask for it, not go there. So act as Superior.

  3. Oh! how distressing! For charity's sake, I rely on your good sense to see that she goes nowhere and sees nothing; you know this already without my telling you.3

  4. Listen, you must send to Pennabilli the one from Invorio whom you clothed, who teaches the boys, and her companion; I think I have explained myself clearly. First you will write to the Superior to let her know, and give them the name of the inn; you can also write two lines to this Gentleman asking him kindly to see the sisters safely onto the mail coach and commend them to the driver.4

  5. In short, my daughter, I urge you to do all you can so that everything goes well. I need the superior;5 try to leave Sr. A. Costanza in the house, near Sr. A. Vincenza, so that if another is needed she can choose whichever she finds most a-

lio

greeable; but I need Sr. A. Santina, because I am unwell and cannot tire myself.6

6. I am sorry to hear you are upset, but I was obliged to give these warnings;7 be of good heart, for it will all end; I cannot write; see how I tremble from weakness.

Goodbye, the Lord bless you; I am your affect. M. R.

1 The letters the Mother mentions have not been preserved. They had certainly gone astray.

2 Cf. L 62,3.

3 You tell me... know this. The lady she speaks of is Sr. A. Vincenza's mother, about whom the Superior, Carlotta, kept complaining. Cf. L to M. Rosa of 1.4.1875.

4 write to the Superior... driver. She gives the instructions with care and precision. Having to spend the night at Rimini, the Sisters usually stayed at Mr Luigi Grossi's inn (we find this name written in the Mother's own hand in a small notebook). AFSA.MaA, Race. 5.

5 Sr. A. Santina. Cf. L62.1.

6 Cf. L 55,6.

7 Cf. L 59.

Contrary to what she wrote earlier, she tells her to stay with Sr. A. Vincenza. She is to ask the Father on what day he is leaving for Genoa.

My daughter,

  1. I wrote to you to come.1 Now I tell you to stay, because I hear from Sr. A. Vincenza's brother that she wants you to remain.2

  2. If the Father decides to come, let him telegraph us, because in one letter he tells me he is coming and in another he is not;3 then in yesterday's he says he is coming on Wednesday, and in this one I have just received he says nothing, so I do not know what to think. Write to me, for you know I understand all your letters.4

Goodbye, your affect. M.

1 Cf. L62,l.

2 Sr. A. Vincenza's condition was getting worse.

3 Father Tornatore, like M. Rosa, was to give sworn testimony requested by A. Ricchino to settle the case. Cf. L 67,2.

4 Sr. A. Santina expressed herself clearly and concisely.

She regrets that her letters have not arrived. Others sent from Piacenza have also gone astray. She would fly to her Vincenza and is distressed at being far away, but she cannot: she is very weak. Onorata is to put «bad» thoughts out of her mind. She will never forget her or her family. Alessandro does not write to her.

A.M.F.

Dear Onorata,

  1. I have just received your letter1 and am replying in my own hand; you tell me of letters you wrote to me which I have not received at all;2 indeed yesterday I said: «how can it be that my Onorata doesn't write to me?» And I was anxious about it.

  2. I am up but very weak, so that I find it hard to write because of the stomach pain I have; I assure you that if I had a little strength I would have flown to my Vincenza, but patience! I assure you I cannot describe to you the pain and anxiety I feel at being far from her.

  3. Carlottina cries all the time, she can't put her mind to anything, and she would like to come and see Sr. A. Vincenza, but how? I don't like letting her come alone, because I am afraid.3

  4. Now allow me to give you a just reproof about your supposed ideas, or rather bad thoughts: that I might forget you and your family, and that my affection and gratitude might fail?!!!!.… Examine yourself a little and then see whether that could happen! No, no, it is among the impossible things! Living and dead, I shall always be grateful and affectionate to you!4

  5. I cannot understand how I have lost all the letters which here in

Piacenza they tell me they sent on the 27th, the 26th and the 28th. I have received none of them. What can it be? I cannot understand it. If you knew how much I suffer in writing and how much I have to write, you would certainly pity me.5

6. I enclose F. 20. Together with the fifty you have, give them to our good mamma with my greetings and tell her many, many things from me. Alessandro does not write!! And yet I wrote to him that it was certainly not up to me to write to him. Patience! It is written that I must drink the whole cup of bitterness; may God's will be done for ever!

Yours, yours for all ages

Affect. Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 The letter she mentions has not been preserved.

2 In those days several letters sent to her from Piacenza had gone astray, as she states below in para. 5. Cf. L 62,3; 63,1.

3 She feared, rightly, that she would meet Sr. A. Vincenza alone, foreseeing the suffering of both.

4 Her friendship with Onorata was deep and lasting, and her relations with the family excellent. Cf. L 37,3.

5 Cf. L 47, n. 3.

She asks her to send two Sisters to Genoa and give them some money. She gives various instructions for the house and asks for prayers.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Listen, first of all don't get it into your head that I am not writing to you; the reason is weakness; I say no more because I really cannot;1 then I want you to send me Sr. A. Albertina and Sr. A. Prassede at once, at once here to Genoa, as I hope you will have sent those for Pennabilli;2 when you send those for Genoa, give them some kitchen linen.

  2. As for wine, buy it, so that what we have will be kept3 for this summer. And if you have collected the F. 500 from the town council, send them to me with the sisters; sew them well into a pocket so that they cannot be seen;4 otherwise, of the F. 500 the Father left you, you can send me 200, if you can, as I have certain expenses to meet for the houses.

  3. Courage, for it is a time to suffer for God. I shall tell you many things by word of mouth.

  4. I hope you will tell me what you are doing about the patient's mattresses and linen;5 and have her room whitewashed and thoroughly cleaned, the tiles too. Listen, as she was not consumptive,6 I would be inclined to have everything washed and then kept for other sick sisters. What do you say?

  5. I would not want anyone to sleep in Carlotta's bed, to spare the poor child distress.

  6. I want you to keep a close eye on Sr. A. Dorotea. You will hear more in person; for charity's sake don't let anything show; she is not to

be too much with Sr. A. Virginia, with Sr. A., the one from Nice.7 Goodbye, the Lord bless you together with the Community, and

She has been informed, regarding the «Ricchino case», that he demands a further statement. She begs him to advise her how to proceed.

Most Rev. Eminence,

  1. How fortunate I would be if I could fly to your feet for advice; as that is not possible, I ask it in writing.

  2. On the third of this month I was notified of the Ricchino judgement, which obliges me to take 17 oaths, all those concerning religion having been left out, and Mr Tornatore 4; so I must either swear or return the money in full.1 I therefore ask Your Most Rev. Eminence, for the good of the work, what it is best to do.2

Having only fifteen days, deign to reply to me; I am sure of obtaining everything from your immense charity at this moment when tribulations are raining down on me in torrents. A word from you will be a comfort to me. Asking your Pastoral blessing, humbled at your feet, I remain Your Most Rev. Eminence's

Most humble Servant Sr. A. Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 On 3 April the Court of Appeal of Genoa published its judgement in the case. M. Rosa was obliged to take oaths on 17 of the 21 points of the previous judgement, 4 having been excluded as concerning her religious activities and not strictly relevant to the subject of the suit. Fr Tornatore was to swear on 4 points instead of 8. Failing this, she would have had to return the money Ricchino offered in 1868 for founding the Institute at Sampierdarena. Cf. L 68, n. 2.

2 The Cardinal replied on 11 April, pointing out that abstaining could prove harmful and encouraging her to appear in Court, as there was no other way to prove her innocence. Cf. AFSA, VW1-6.

Regarding the «Ricchino lawsuit», she has been notified that she is called to testify under oath. She awaits his advice before making her decision.

Most Rev. Eminence,

  1. Since I cannot come myself to humble myself at your feet for advice in a most important matter, I must use the pen, sure that by this means too I shall receive the same answer from your immense charity, of which I have had no few proofs.1

  2. Your Eminence knows well that the work of Saint Anne has a lawsuit, and after I have won it several times,2 now, since my opponent can find no other means, it imposes oaths on me: either to swear or to return the money he had given me to open a House seven years ago3 (which still exists), with many girls and nuns, many of the girls having been placed there by that Priest and kept free of charge.

  3. Now I wish to know how I should proceed, as I have only a few days to reply.4

  4. For pity's sake, Your Eminence, do not leave me without an answer, which I await before taking any decision.

Your Pastoral blessing comforts me; may it support me in so many adversities.

Most humble Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

1 The reply is dated 12 April. AFSA, PC1M 75-1.

A girl placed in the Institute by the «Province» has been wrongly sent away. She regrets it and suggests how to put it right.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I am extremely sorry about what has happened with the girl from the Province, when I had told you not to send away any of the Province's girls, because we could not, you know that; so how did it happen?1

  2. So take her back at once, go to the Prefect and tell him it was a mistake, as it was thought she had been placed by other people, the registers not having been checked at all and memory relied on.2

  3. «She is certainly extremely bad, but we are taking her back, and if after this trial she does not change we shall inform Your Excellency so that you may think of placing her elsewhere».

  4. Meanwhile have her taken at once to the Morte,3 and then the Father will tell you more in person.4

  5. Go at once to the Prefect, fetch the girl at once and take her to the Morte; as for the teacher, leave her free.5 For charity's sake, before sending girls away, think about what you are doing so as not to get into a mess.

  6. You know I have always told you about the Province's girls: we cannot touch them or send them away without a serious reason and without informing the Commission.

Goodbye for now; take courage, don't worry; your

affect. M. R. P.S. Before sending any girls away, let me know.

dalla

1 The Superior had sent away from the Institute a girl «supported» Province of Piacenza, without informing the competent Commission.

2 That she had been placed and supported by other people; she had not consulted the attendance registers.

3 To the House in Via della Morte. 4 Fr Tornatore, on his return from Genoa, would explain the matter to her.

The Inspector wishes to take a girl from the Institute into service in his home. She tells her which one to send and how to handle it. Some postulants will be arriving. She asks her to clothe the suitable postulants.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just received another letter in which I hear that the Inspector wants an older girl for service; for this we must make the sacrifice of giving him one. Listen, you know that when we spoke of this matter we had agreed to give him Rosina; I think she is the strong one who taught at the Morte, and she would go willingly.

  2. Tell this lady that it is being done for her,1 but that it would not have been done for anyone else, as she is a girl we need; but for them we would do anything; and if she does not suit, we shall take her back.2

  3. Then give the girl plenty of good advice;3 tell her to come and see you often and to behave well; in short, that if she is good she may come back whenever she no longer wants to stay there; that will encourage her. I hope you received my letter of yesterday in which I spoke to you at length about the Prefect.4

  4. I want you to clothe all the postulants, meaning those you think are really suited to be clothed;5 one I should like to be the one from Bologna, as I need her. Clothe them at once. In a few days another will reach you from Ovada, but she is a good one, and also one from S. Martinello, and she will come together with Sr. A. Aprotozina;6 you understand me without my explaining further.

Goodbye for now, your affect. M. R.

1 To this lady, that is, the school Inspector's wife, that an exception is being made for her.

2 If she does not suit: if she does not find her suitable.

3 plenty of good advice: many important recommendations.

4 It is letter 69.

5 The Register of Novices shows no clothing in April 1875.

6 Sr. A. Protasina Bellotti.

She has learned of a Priest's visit to the Mother House to make arrangements for the new house to be opened in the Diocese. As she is away, she will deal with the matter by letter.

Most Rev. Excellency,

1. I received your esteemed letter and, to my great regret, did not have the good fortune to be in Piacenza when the excellent Priest went there to agree on the negotiations for a house in your Diocese.2 I am therefore writing to this Curate,3 that if he wishes to come to an arrangement we can use the pen just as well as speaking in person.

2. I therefore warmly thank Your Most Rev. Excellency for having deigned to admit us to the number of your flock, unworthy as we are to be so.

Deign to grant me your Pastoral Blessing as, full of devotion, I declare myself

Most humble Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 The date is inferred from an L of the Archbishop to M. Rosa of 8 April 1875, in which he specified: «The bearer of this letter will be the Priest Fr Giovanni Brugioni, chaplain of Palagano... his parish priest is sending him to make the necessary arrangements».

2 The excellent Priest is Fr Giovanni Brugioni.

3 The curate is Fr Domenico Zanni.

The Bishop's letter about opening an FSA House has been forwarded to her from Piacenza. As she is away, she asks him to state by letter the number of Sisters and the grade of certificate required for the teacher.

Rev. Archpriest,

  1. I have received, through the Superior in Piacenza, a letter from the Archbishop of Parma delivered by Your Reverence, concerning arrangements for the mission of the Daughters of Saint Anne in your Parish.2

  2. As I have to remain here for some time, if Your Reverence will kindly deal with this matter by letter, we shall continue, God willing. I enclose my address.

  3. Please let me know the number of Religious, also the grade of the teacher,3 and the stipend. On receiving this I shall do all I can to satisfy you.

  4. Meanwhile I thank you for turning your gaze upon us, most unworthy creatures who with God's help desire nothing but to do a little good for humanity. Bless me and believe me, as I remain

Your humble Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 Cf. L71.1.

2 It is L 71, from the Abp. of Modena, not of Parma. In his Parish, at Palagano.

3 The teacher's grade. For the first three classes a «lower grade» certificate was required; for the 4th and 5th, a «higher grade» one.

As a tangible proof of affection, she asks her to make the sacrifice of giving up going to Piacenza. She herself will go to Rome to stay «a good while» with her dear daughters.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Just a line, although I am weighed down with work. Listen, now is the moment to show me by deeds what you have always told me in words and in writing: the love you bear both me and the Institute. So you must make the sacrifice of staying at the Parrocchietta and, for this year, not coming to Piacenza.1

  1. By October, God willing, I shall be in your arms to stay a good while; so, my daughter, answer me at once to console me and tell me that you are my beloved daughter who wants to be submissive and obedient in everything.2

  2. Receive this letter of mine cheerfully; I shall judge of that from your reply, which I await with the greatest longing. God bless you, I implore it with all my soul, while I tell you I am weighed down with work and so can go on no longer.

I am your Affect. M. R.

1 Sr. A. Irene, one of the first cholera orphans taken into the Mother House, was devoted to her and wanted to be near her through letters and sometimes in person, by going to Piacenza. At the Parrocchietta: a school, today in Via del Casaletto.

2 ...answer me at once. She wants her dear daughter to grow in freedom through the responsible and joyful acceptance of the sacrifice she was asking of her for the sake of a greater good.

Being separated from her costs her not a little. She begs her to take care of herself and write with news of her health.

I

I A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

  1. Just a line to show you that I am on my feet. Dear daughter, being separated from you costs me not a little.1 Alas! Take care of yourself, for pity's sake, for my only consolation is to hear that you are well; I can bear no more wounds.2 Have pity on one whom I know you love and who returns your affection beyond measure, your Affect. Mother.

  2. Write to me, otherwise I shall be anxious. Did the trip to Genoa do you harm? Tell me the truth, do you understand?3 Oh! how many things I would have to tell you. Oh! where am I? I no longer seem to belong to this earth.4 Dear daughter, I greet you and hold you close to me, as I am your

affect. M.

1 She had had to leave her at Sampierdarena, because her commitments for the work of God required her presence in Piacenza.

2 Take care... wounds. This is an urgent exhortation. The Sisters' illnesses and recently Sr. A. Vincenza's death had laid her low.

3 From Sampierdarena she had gone to Genoa. She wanted to know whether it had harmed her, so that she could go on entrusting her with errands in Genoa.

4 How many things... earth? After Sr. A. Vincenza's death she has only her left, the one person to whom she can confide the secrets of the Work of God. She feels the emptiness Vincenza has left, cannot believe she is gone; she feels detached, a stranger to the earth.

She thanks him for his kindness to the FSA and for finding a house better suited to their work. She asks him to obtain the Cardinal's approval and the Holy Father's blessing. She will inform the Superior of the house in Trastevere.

Most Rev. Excellency,

  1. I reply to your esteemed letter, which I received just now, on the 20th of this month.1 First of all I must say that I am exceedingly ashamed not to have written to Your Most Rev. Excellency before now to thank you for all the care and attention you give to the poor Daughters of Saint Anne. My incapacity cannot express how much gratitude I feel towards so great a benefactor. God will repay you.

  2. As for the House, I am ready to make some small sacrifice, and I would make it more generously if I could have a single line from the Cardinal letting me know that it is his wish that the Daughters of Saint Anne should occupy those premises.2

  3. Most Rev. Monsignor, what do you say to this wish of mine? Is it perhaps too bold? If so, give me a good scolding, which I shall gladly accept. Do you know what makes me so frank? It is your kindness, and it gives me courage to tell you freely and in all confidence what I would like and what would be a real consolation to me; it would encourage me to undertake this matter!

  4. And also if a blessing of the Holy Father could be had; for the rest, being sure of obtaining what I put to you, go ahead and secure the house, for I am writing now to the Superior in Trastevere to inform her of everything.3

  5. If my health had not tied me down, I would certainly have come to Rome before now, but this year I shall certainly not be able to come. If it pleases God to keep me alive, next year I shall have

the happiness of being at your feet, and we shall continue the negotiations for the nuns you mention better in person.

6. I always look forward to your letters, however, which are very dear to me, dealing as they do with matters concerning the Work of the Lord.

Bless me, while full of veneration I remain, Most Rev. Monsignor, your

Humble Servant Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

1 The L is dated 17 April 1875. Cf. AFSA CpIC, Roma, 3. He proposes premises in the Conservatorio Borromeo, in the Rione Monti, very suitable for the Sisters. A devout lady is willing to contribute monthly towards the rent. The Mother replies that she is ready to make some small sacrifice.

2 ...I would make it more generously... premises. This wish implies a fact Mgr. Gentili did not state. The Superior, Domenica Marchesini, had not only given her very favourable opinion of the premises but had foreseen a future development: she had been told that the Cardinal Vicar and also the Holy Father wanted the FSA in those premises, as they could later take over the running of the orphanage directed by the Borromean Sisters (the Congregation of Sisters occupying part of the palazzo).

3 The Superior, Domenica Marchesini, was directly concerned in the transfer of her community from the Rione Trastevere.

As she must submit an application for three girls to be admitted to hospital, she asks her to write down their names exactly.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

1. Send me by Francesco2 the names of the three girls who are to go to hospital, which you forgot to copy out for me last night: one is that little one with scrofula, the other the one who was at the Morte, and the other the one called Tisin. Goodbye. Be sure to get it right, because I have to send it to the Town Hall now. Be quick, just first names and surnames.

Goodbye, I embrace you.

[M. R.]

1 From its content and context it is assumed to have been written in Piacenza — the House in Via della Morte — after her return from Genoa.

2 The gardener of the Mother House.

She has received her letters. She will soon have to go to Genoa and will tell her of the «sorrows of the Work of Saint Anne». So she merely gives some urgent instructions about a girl and the postulants.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received your two letters.1 Ah! dear daughter, how many sorrows there are in the work of Saint Anne! Enough, everything by word of mouth, because from what I hear from Accinelli I shall certainly not be long;2 be prepared to hear some fine things such as you have certainly never heard yet.

  2. I am fairly well, but I wish the same were true of you; don't be surprised if I write little, but you will understand how much I have to do.

  3. Listen, have Paolina3 brought to you and hear what she has to say, for I am told she does not want to stay there any longer; if so, tell her to be calm, for at the first opportunity you will have her taken to Piacenza.

  4. As for the postulant, mind, I absolutely do not want postulants to stay at S. P. d'Arena; they must come here because I want to test them; and see that they have all their papers, both the doctor's and their birth certificates.4 Goodbye.

  5. For your guidance: when you send sisters with postulants, note that the railway will not accept postulants' seats at half fare.5 I am writing in such a rush that I don't know whether you will understand me; I am even perched on the corner of a table.6 So much business! Goodbye. God bless you,

your affect. M.R.

1 They are dated 22 and 25 April.

2 Regarding the Ricchino case, Fr Accinelli had told her on 17.4.1875: «The summons for the oaths has been served; today the doctor's certificate was drawn up and on Monday it will be presented to the Court with a request that they be taken at home. Next Saturday (24.4) the day will be fixed, and I shall let you know at once».

3 Cf. L 23, n. 3-4.

4 A young woman from Turin had applied. Fr Accinelli had mentioned her in the L referred to above.

5 They will not take them at half fare. Postulants were not granted the 50% reduction on train journeys.

6 She is writing leaning on the corner of the table.

Instructions about the Vernengo Sisters, who want to leave the Institute, and about the girl Paolina.

My daughter,

  1. I have received your letter and telegraphed you at once; now I repeat by letter: do not let the Vernengo sisters go out dressed as Religious even for half an hour unless they have first spoken to Fr Accinelli, whom I have also telegraphed to come and hear how matters stand.1

  2. As for Paolina, when there is an opportunity for Piacenza, send her; tell her I hear that she wants it, and so I shall have her taken home.2 Do you understand? What a blessed house, there is always something. Patience! The Lord permits it so; His will be done. Goodbye, your

Affect. M. R.

1 The Vernengo sisters: cf. L 14, n. 2.

2 Cf. L 77, 3.

She asks her to deliver this letter to the superior of the Sampierdarena House, with her further order regarding the Vernengo sisters.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Send this letter at once and see: the Vernengo ladies want to leave, but in the habit of Saint Anne, and I would be very sorry about that. I have telegraphed Fr Accinelli and the Superior of the house; how she wanted... my God, how dreadful!2

  2. These days, what goings-on! Enough, in person. How are you? For pity's sake take care of yourself, for you need it. I assure you.3 Your affect.

M. R. Gattorno

1 The date is inferred from its connection with the previous letter (no. 78), which is referred to here and which it accompanies.

2 Cf. L78.1.

3 Take care of yourself: she never tires of repeating it, as she was well aware of her state of health and of the great work she did in the hospital without sparing herself.

She tells him of the illness and death of Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino. A short biography of her will be compiled as soon as possible.

A.M.F. My Father,

  1. A line in my own hand in reply to yours, which was most welcome. God gave me a Creature after His own Heart and all zeal for His Work; He has taken her from me; fiat.1

  2. She died a saint, as she lived virtuously; her illness was a continual sleep of paradise, mysterious even to the doctors; her death a most gentle sleep, wholly absorbed in the most blessed Virgin.2

  3. The sacrifice of separation, of not being able to see each other again on this earth, was accepted with such resignation that it is admirable.3 A short life will soon be put together, and her illness will be described in detail.4

  4. My Father, I shall not write at length, because I have no small stomach ache; may all the suffering of this poor servant of His be for my God. I am your

Humble Devoted Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 She is speaking of Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino, who died on 3 April 1875.

2 She died on a Saturday, the day dedicated to the Virgin.

3 She had indeed been unable to go to her, for health reasons and also because she was busy with the settlement of the Ricchino case. Cf. L 67 and 68.

4 The short biography was written by Onorata Colli and printed in Piacenza by Tip. Favari e Breda in 1875.

She has received his letter and is grateful for his warnings and advice about Carlotta. She gives explanations and will explain more fully in person.

My Most Rev. Father,

  1. Yesterday I received your esteemed letter, which I read with real pleasure. How could you doubt, my Father, that I might be annoyed by a warning from you? Ah, no! on the contrary, I am most grateful and thank Your Paternity for so charitably giving me good advice.1

  2. If you will allow me, I should like (not to justify myself) but only to clarify what you were told. Listen: first of all, regarding the girl, I took advice in Rome from [your] Fathers,2 and so did she from her Confessor, Mgr. Mariano, Secretary to His Eminence.3

  3. As for the dinners, I have examined myself4 and do not know when I can have given dinners; only the Mamma of poor Sister A. Vincenza stayed here in this House, and she was certainly treated as her position required; she did not fail to leave the house a large alms.5 Otherwise we have had no outsiders in the house since then.

  4. Well, God permits it; His will be done. I hope to explain everything better to you in person, and then you, my Father, will see whether it is something that could give scandal, a word whose very name makes me tremble.6

Pray, my Father, for me and for my children, and believe me ever your

Most humble and Most devoted Servant Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

1 She shows humility and magnanimity, calmly weighing what she has been told, while aware that the «rumours» reported to her about Carlotta and herself were unfounded.

2 She sought advice in Rome from the Jesuit Fathers.

3 Carlotta for her part followed the advice of her spiritual Father, Mgr. Mariano Wanstienkist, secretary to Cardinal Luigi Vannicelli Casoni.

4 I have examined myself: I have tried to remember and examine my conscience.

5 Signora Bianca Rapallino had stayed as a guest to nurse her sick daughter. Cf. L 59,3.

6 She is ready and willing to go through the accusations against her point by point: she is perfectly at peace; she is sorry only for any offence to God. In this case, having given occasion for «scandal», a bad example.

Pleased with the good news, she asks whether a debt has been paid off. She is to send the decoction. She will give her news in person of her father and sister, who came to visit her.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I am delighted with the good news that you have paid both for the mattresses and the bill; I should like to know whether you still owe Fr Accinelli anything.1 Oh! what a consolation to hear that you are free of debt and that you have sick people.2 God be blessed!

  2. I should like you to send me a little more of the decoction, both for me and for the Father; tell Signora Maddalena that this last lot did us a great deal of good, so that she knows what to do.3 Send it to me as soon as you can.

  3. Your sister came, but it was odd: she and your father both said that he does not want to leave her, because he wanted her always to be with you. Enough, you will hear in person; what an odd man he is!4

Goodbye. Greet everyone for me and believe me your

affect. M.R.

1 She had cleared a large debt: the mattresses and the cloth bought for the Sisters' habits.

2 That you have sick people to nurse and care for.

3 Cf. L 57, n. 5.

4 Her father, with her sister, had gone to visit her, but the sister had not stayed in Piacenza as a postulant. Both wanted her to be with Sr. A. Santina. The young woman entered the FSA on 16.10.1876 and received the habit on 5.11.1876 with the name Sr. A. Grimalda.

She hears that she has had another haemorrhage. If the day set for the «oaths» is still some way off, she is to ask for eight days' leave and come to Piacenza to rest. She will return to Sampierdarena with her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Just a line, because I am so busy that I don't know which way to turn. Listen, you tell me you have brought up blood again;1 well, I would suggest that you see whether there is still time before the oaths; if so you could ask for 8 [days'] leave and come and stay with me, and then we shall go back to Genoa together, so you could have a little rest.2

  2. As for the confessor, listen, I think you should go and beg the parish priest of S.P. d'Arena to come himself; you will see that you will be pleased; what do you say? Oh! for pity's sake let us leave the others alone;3 enough, you will hear everything in person. So go to the parish priest and beg him earnestly to accept; when he has accepted, go to the Archbishop and tell him. I can't wait to embrace you. Goodbye; come

your affect. M.R.

1 Sr. A. Francesca suffered from chronic tracheitis.

2 For the oaths: cf. L 67, n. 1; 77, n. 2.

3 As for the confessor. The confessor of the Pietrine Sisters had no time for the FSA, nor was it advisable to call on that of the Madri Pie. So Sr. A. Francesca asked the Mother what to do. Cf. L 30.4.1875. Her answer is precise: she is to approach the Parish Priest of Sampierdarena and leave the other Sisters' confessors alone.

She answers her question about the price of eggs.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Yesterday I received yours,1 in which you ask me to tell you how much eggs cost; at the last market, last Saturday, the price was 5 centimes an egg; in fact I bought thirty and gave her a little less, four and a half centimes each, and if one buys more they would come even cheaper. I don't know; then you have the toll, but perhaps since it is for the hospital they won't make you pay it.

  2. I hope you received my letter in which I told you many things;2 as for the Vernengo sisters, you did well to advise her so.3 I can't wait to see you; I hope you will come and spend the feast days with me here in Piacenza.

Goodbye, yours in haste

affect. M. R.

1 On the 3rd of this month she told her that the Board of Management had decided to manage the housekeeping better. She had been asked to see to buying eggs, ordering them from Piacenza, where they cost less.

2 It is L 83.

3 Regarding the Vernengo sisters (cf. L 14, n. 2), she had advised the Superior, Elisabetta, to be firm. If they wanted to leave the Institute they must first lay aside the FSA habit.

She tells him the date of a novice's death. Regarding the warnings about Carlotta, she reports the opinion of people she has consulted. She will speak to him about the matter in person.

Most Rev. Father,

  1. Yesterday I received your esteemed letter, in which I found a just complaint against me. It is quite true that I have been negligent.1 My God! what an abyss of imperfections I am... The mass of my occupations keeps me from fulfilling my most heartfelt duties.

  2. So, on 30 April at 5 p.m. the very dear soul of Sister A. Evangelista flew to heaven.2

  3. My Father, now allow me to tell you quite frankly what I told the excellent Marquis Landi when he spoke to me about Sister A. Evangelista. I told him these exact words: I wanted to send her away, and I made representations to Father Santi, who was the one who placed her; but as I am under so many obligations to this Father, I could not help giving in and keeping her, because it is quite true that when they fall ill in the year of novitiate we send them away, but out of regard for Father Santi, to whom I am so indebted, I kept her. Do let the Marchioness3 read these words of mine and you will see whether it is true or not.

  4. Listen, my Father, in these days I have tried asking people of high standing whether what my daughter was doing could give scandal.4 They answered that no one had ever said anything, and that everyone was quite convinced that the poor, unfortunate girl should be able to have a little distraction.

  5. I mentioned the people she goes about with: excellent, they told me. My Father, as for the dinner with the Counts Marazzani,5 this is a downright lie: the girls came one day and stayed until late, and Carlottina let them share the frugal meal, if it can be called

a dinner. I really took no notice [of] this nonsense; what do you say?

  1. Listen, my Father, since you give me such freedom to speak, you see, in Piacenza there are a great many people who have never done anything for our poor Institute! I shall tell you the rest in person; only Marquis Alfonso, he indeed has always given and helped me; the others of the family, nothing.

  2. In Piacenza too I have kept, as always, 150 girls, at our own expense, and always nursing of the sick, but very few have contributed, and elsewhere I have always found them.

  3. I hope to be able to tell you everything better in person; meanwhile forgive me, bless me, and believe me ever

Most humble Servant Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

1 She had not answered his letter promptly.

2 Sr. A. Evangelista Antoniazzi had received the religious habit on 21 March 1875.

3 The excellent Marquis Alfonso Landi. He may by all means let the Marchioness Teresa Landi Bellini read the letter.

4 Cf. L81.

5 The family of Count Camillo Marazzani liked to have Carlotta as a guest.

She sends her the letter to be handed to the Superior, Elisabetta, and repeats the invitation to come to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

Give this letter of mine to Sr. A. Elisabetta at once;1 I hope to see you soon

your most Affect. M. R.

Come, I am expecting you; take no notice of the telegram, because I am away only for a short time; otherwise I am expecting you. Enough, in person.

1 She encloses the letter published next.

For the problem regarding the Vernengo sisters that she raised, she is to turn to Fr Accinelli and not worry.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received yours and hear what you tell me about the Vernengo sisters.1 Listen, tell them that in a few days I shall be [there] again2 and that if they have anything to say they should go to Fr Accinelli, for I shall approve whatever he does.

  2. And don't you fret; be of good heart and do everything for God; a brief suffering is little for an eternity of joy.3

Your affect. M., who wishes you a thousand blessings from Heaven, while I am your

affect. M. R.

1 The letter she refers to has not been preserved.

2 Tell the Vernengo sisters that I shall be back in Genoa in a few days. Cf. L 84, n. 3.

3 The situation of these two sisters worried the Superior a great deal because of the uneasy atmosphere they created in the community.

She has received the money order and has promptly had the eggs bought and sent. She is waiting to be called; she will soon be in Genoa.

A.M.F. My Francesca,

  1. I received yours with the money order for F 20 and at once sent to the market for the eggs, which are already on their way; I enclose the dispatch note.1

  2. I hear about your troubles and am very sorry, but listen, remember that they are trifles that vanish with an hour's calm.

  3. You will have received my note; stand firm with everyone, for I shall soon be there, as is true, because every day I am waiting to be called;2 tell no one that I am in Piacenza, and if they ask you, say you know I was due to leave. For charity's sake, it would be the last straw if the Vernengo sisters came to Piacenza; we have enough already.3

  4. You told me a basket was coming; for your information, we have received nothing; and I tell you not to send any more vegetables, because now there are plenty in Piacenza and there is a risk that I won't even eat them, as there are so many that the community eats them too. Goodbye. In haste, your

Affect. M.

1 Cf. L. 84.

2 Cf. L. 86. You can confirm the news of my arrival there, because I am waiting to be called by Fr Accinelli. Cf. L 77, n. 2.

3 She had entrusted Accinelli with handling the financial side of the annuity.

She is pleased with the good news of the house. When the beds have arrived, in agreement with the Superior and the Duchess, they can go to Oppello to put the house in order.
